name: Battle of Waterloo
info: On 18 June 1815 a French army under Napoleon was defeated near Waterloo, in present-day Belgium, by a British-led army under Wellington and a Prussian army under Blücher; Napoleon abdicated again four days later.

facts.date: 18 June 1815 (a Sunday); the time the fighting began is uncertain
facts.place: The ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, about 2 kilometres from Waterloo and 15 kilometres south of Brussels, in the municipalities of Braine-l'Alleud and Lasne, in present-day Belgium (then the United Kingdom of the Netherlands)
facts.sides: The French Imperial Army (Armée du Nord) under Napoleon, about 74,500 men with 254 guns; an Anglo-allied army under Wellington, 74,326 men with 156 guns, from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Hanover, Brunswick and Nassau; a Prussian army under Blücher, of which about 48,000 men in two and a half corps were engaged
facts.outcome: The French army was routed and the Imperial Guard repulsed after the Prussians broke through on the French right. Napoleon announced his second abdication on 24 June 1815.

t: Napoleon meant to defeat the Prussian and Anglo-allied armies separately, but the Prussians withdrew north to Wavre and marched back to join Wellington, while the 33,000 men Napoleon had sent after them were held up at Wavre.

Wellington's army stood on a ridge through the afternoon against French infantry, cavalry and artillery, and the Imperial Guard was repulsed in the evening as the Prussians broke through on the French right.
Wellington lost around 17,000 dead or wounded, Blücher some 7,000 and Napoleon 24,000 to 26,000 killed or wounded, with a further 15,000 deserting afterwards.
dyk: Wellington's dispatch put the start of the French attack on Hougoumont at about ten o'clock, other sources say around 11:30, and the historian Andrew Roberts notes that no one is absolutely certain when the battle began.
ev: The powers at the Congress of Vienna declare Napoleon an outlaw and the United Kingdom, Russia, Austria and Prussia mobilise armies against him
The French cross the frontier near Charleroi before dawn on 15 June
Napoleon defeats the Prussians at Ligny while Ney fights Wellington's forces at Quatre Bras on 16 June
Wellington withdraws to the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean and the Prussians fall back to Wavre on 17 June
The Anglo-allied army holds the ridge against French attacks from late morning until the Imperial Guard is repulsed at about 19:30
Wellington and Blücher meet near La Belle Alliance at around 21:00 and the Prussians pursue the French through the night
Napoleon announces his second abdication on 24 June
Napoleon surrenders to Captain Frederick Maitland of HMS Bellerophon on 15 July, and is later exiled to Saint Helena

sections.background:
On 13 March 1815, six days before Napoleon reached Paris, the powers at the Congress of Vienna declared him an outlaw. Four days later the United Kingdom, Russia, Austria and Prussia mobilised armies against him. Napoleon was critically outnumbered, and his only chance of staying in power was to attack before the coalition had mobilised. By June he had raised a total army strength of about 300,000 men, but the force at his disposal at Waterloo was less than one third of that. He planned to strike Wellington's and Blücher's armies one after the other, before they could join and invade France.

The French crossed the frontier near Charleroi before dawn on 15 June. On 16 June Napoleon defeated Blücher at Ligny, while Ney's left wing fought Wellington's forces at Quatre Bras, where the Anglo-allied army held its ground but could not reinforce the Prussians. The Prussians did not retreat eastwards along their own lines of communication. They fell back northwards, parallel to Wellington, and rallied near Wavre. On 17 June Wellington withdrew to the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, a position he had reconnoitred the year before. Napoleon had ordered Grouchy to follow the Prussians with 33,000 men; a late start, uncertainty about the direction the Prussians had taken and vague orders meant he was too late to stop them reaching Wavre. Early on 18 June Wellington received Blücher's assurance of support and decided to give battle.
sections.forces:
The French army numbered around 74,500: 54,014 infantry, 15,830 cavalry and 8,775 artillerymen with 254 guns. Napoleon had not conscripted men for the 1815 campaign, and the troops were mainly veterans devoted to him. Officers were allocated to units as they presented themselves, so that many were commanded by men the soldiers did not know, and some of these officers had little experience of working together.

Wellington's army was 74,326 strong: 53,607 infantry, 13,400 cavalry and 5,596 artillerymen with 156 guns. Of these 27,985 (38 per cent) were British, 7,686 were from the King's German Legion, 21,035 Dutch-Belgian and Nassau troops, 11,496 from Hanover and 6,124 from Brunswick. Wellington later called it "an infamous army, very weak and ill-equipped". Many of the coalition troops were inexperienced, though the historian Alessandro Barbero states that the difference between British and foreign troops did not prove significant under fire. About 17,000 more were stationed at Halle as a guard against a wide flanking movement. Two and a half Prussian corps, or 48,000 men, were engaged, led by an excellent and professional general staff.

Wellington drew his infantry up behind the crest of a ridge, hiding it on the reverse slope, with the farm of Hougoumont on his right, La Haye Sainte in front of his centre and Papelotte on his left. Napoleon, who could not see Wellington's positions, drew up his forces symmetrically about the Brussels road and later delegated command on the field to Ney.
sections.course:
Napoleon delayed the start because of the sodden ground. At Hougoumont Wellington's dispatch put the first attack at about ten o'clock; other sources say around 11:30. The fighting there lasted all afternoon, and the house held until the end. The French grande batterie of 80 guns opened fire at 11:50 according to Lord Hill, other sources giving between noon and 13:30. At about 13:15 Napoleon saw Prussian columns near Lasne-Chapelle-Saint-Lambert. A little after 13:00 d'Erlon's I Corps advanced against Wellington's left and was met and driven back by the British heavy cavalry, which captured two eagles and then suffered heavy losses.

A little before 16:00 Ney saw movement behind Wellington's centre and mistook the removal of casualties for a retreat. He sent in cavalry, around 9,000 in 67 squadrons at the largest, against infantry squares, which British witnesses recorded as 12 assaults. Later the French took La Haye Sainte, partly because the King's German Legion's ammunition ran out, and their guns and skirmishers then pressed Wellington's centre at short range. From 16:30 the Prussian IV Corps attacked towards Plancenoit, and Zieten's I Corps reached Wellington's left.

At around 19:30 Napoleon committed the Imperial Guard. It appears to have been five battalions of the Middle Guard, with three Old Guard battalions in support. The attack was repulsed, and as the cry "La Garde recule" spread, Wellington waved his hat to signal a general advance. The Prussians took Plancenoit, which changed hands five times, and the French army broke.
sections.aftermath:
Wellington lost around 17,000 dead or wounded and Blücher some 7,000. Napoleon's losses were 24,000 to 26,000 killed or wounded, including 6,000 to 7,000 captured, with an additional 15,000 deserting afterwards. Coalition cavalry harried the fugitives until about 23:00, and Gneisenau pursued them as far as Genappe, where Napoleon's carriage was captured. By then 78 guns and 2,000 prisoners had been taken. A visitor to the field on 22 June wrote that the heaps of wounded men with mangled limbs were perishing from lack of dressing or food, and that the wounded of both sides remained in a deplorable state. Tens of thousands of the dead were later stripped of teeth, which were sold as the so-called Waterloo teeth for dentures.

Grouchy defeated Thielmann at Wavre on 19 June and withdrew in good order, but 33,000 French troops had not reached the field. Napoleon reached Paris on 21 June. His support from the public and his own army waned, and he announced his second abdication on 24 June. Coalition forces advanced on Paris and entered it on 7 July. Napoleon surrendered to Captain Frederick Maitland of HMS Bellerophon on 15 July, was exiled to Saint Helena and died there in 1821. Louis XVIII was restored, and the Treaty of Paris was signed on 20 November 1815.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from many participants' accounts. Wellington's dispatch of 19 June was published in the London Gazette on 22 June. Others come from the British gunner Captain Mercer, an unnamed officer of the Foot Guards, Chassé, Napoleon's memoirs, the Prussian liaison officer Müffling and later writers such as Jomini and Clausewitz, who served in the campaign. These accounts disagree, and some have been questioned. Uxbridge said the Dutch carabiniers refused to follow him, but no Dutch or Belgian source supports this. The Guard's reply "La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas" is called apocryphal, and Hugo's report of a remark by Wellington about the altered field was never documented.

Historians dispute details. Roberts says no one is certain when the battle began. Casualties of the cavalry brigades were noted only for the battle as a whole, so the figures are estimates, and Barbero holds that the rolls overstate the numbers present. Chandler and others hold that the British heavy cavalry were destroyed as a force after their first charge, while Clark-Kennedy and Wood describe their continuing service. Which Guard units made the final attack was also unclear.

Archaeology adds little. Only two complete skeletons had been found by 2022: a Hanoverian soldier of the King's German Legion in 2012 and another in a ditch near a field hospital, with a few partial remains since. Wilkin, Schäfer and Pollard conclude that local farmers dug up the dead and sold the bones to the Waterloo sugar factory to make bone-char.
sections.legacy:
Each generation in Europe up to the First World War saw Waterloo as the turning point that ushered in the Concert of Europe, followed by almost four decades without a major international conflict until the Crimean War of 1853 to 1856. It ended the First French Empire and the wars that had convulsed Europe since the 1790s. The settlement included the Holy Alliance and a German Confederation increasingly dominated by Prussia.

Opinions on the cause of the result differ. Jomini named Blücher's arrival, the firmness of the British infantry, the weather and the formation of the first corps. Clausewitz attributed Napoleon's fall to mistakes, recklessness and overreaching ambition. Wellington credited the Prussian operation against the French flank as most decisive, a view Clausewitz did not share. Parkinson holds that neither army beat Napoleon alone.

The Grenadier Guards took their title and bearskins in the belief that they had beaten the Old Guard grenadiers, the Household Cavalry adopted the cuirass in 1821, and Britain converted its first lancer regiment in 1816. In 1820 King William I of the Netherlands ordered the Lion's Mound, built from 300,000 cubic metres of earth taken from the ridge. The phrase "meeting one's Waterloo" has come to mean a catastrophic reversal. Belgium's 2015 bicentenary two-euro coin was withdrawn after France protested.

summary: The Battle of Waterloo, fought on 18 June 1815, ended Napoleon's Hundred Days. A British-led army under Wellington held a ridge south of Brussels until the Prussians under Blücher attacked the French flank and the Imperial Guard was repulsed.
references: Alessandro Barbero, The Battle: A New History of Waterloo (Atlantic Books, 2005)
Tim Clayton, Waterloo, Four Days that Changed Europe's Destiny (Little, Brown Book Group Limited., 2015)
Andrew W. Field, Waterloo The French Perspective (Pen & Sword Books, 2013)
David Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (New York: Macmillan, 1966)
Ian Fletcher, A Desperate Business: Wellington, The British Army and the Waterloo Campaign (Spellmount, 2001)
notes: Prussian strength: the lead says 50,000 arrived progressively; the Armies section says 48,000 were engaged. I used 48,000 in facts and forces.
Start of the fighting at Hougoumont: Wellington says about ten o'clock, others 11:30; grande batterie 11:50 to 13:30. Both given.

The article says the Prussians reached Wavre and Grouchy was held there; it also says 33,000 French troops never reached the field (the number Grouchy was sent after the Prussians with). Both uses follow the article.
The date of the coalition entry into Paris (7 July) comes only from the lead.

Cavalry losses (1,205 troopers and 1,303 horses of 2,651 official strength) were left out because the article says all such figures are estimates; the Old Guard and Young Guard losses (Young Guard 96 per cent) were also left out for space.
The article has no section on sources; the sources section is assembled from its remarks on accounts, disputes and archaeology.
